claim: Sensory hair cells in the ear utilize specialized ribbon synapses.
source: Sensory hair cells in the ear utilize specialized ribbon synapses.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about hair cell synapses.

claim: Ribbon synapses are defined by electron-dense presynaptic structures called ribbons, composed primarily of the structural protein Ribeye.
source: These synapses are defined by electron-dense presynaptic structures called ribbons, composed primarily of the structural protein Ribeye.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of ribbon synapses.

claim: Voltage-gated influx of Ca2+ through CaV1.3 channels is critical for hair-cell synapse function.
source: Previous work has shown that voltage-gated influx of Ca2+ through CaV1.3 channels is critical for hair-cell synapse function and can impede ribbon formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Voltage-gated influx of Ca2+ through CaV1.3 channels can impede ribbon formation.
source: Previous work has shown that voltage-gated influx of Ca2+ through CaV1.3 channels is critical for hair-cell synapse function and can impede ribbon formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mature zebrafish hair cells, evoked presynaptic-Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels initiates mitochondrial-Ca2+ uptake adjacent to ribbons.
source: We show that in mature zebrafish hair cells, evoked presynaptic-Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels initiates mitochondrial-Ca2+ (mito-Ca2+) uptake adjacent to ribbons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Block of mito-Ca2+ uptake in mature cells depresses presynaptic-Ca2+ influx.
source: Block of mito-Ca2+ uptake in mature cells depresses presynaptic-Ca2+ influx and impacts synapse integrity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Block of mito-Ca2+ uptake in mature cells impacts synapse integrity.
source: Block of mito-Ca2+ uptake in mature cells depresses presynaptic-Ca2+ influx and impacts synapse integrity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: In developing zebrafish hair cells, mito-Ca2+ uptake coincides with spontaneous rises in presynaptic-Ca2+ influx.
source: In developing zebrafish hair cells, mito-Ca2+ uptake coincides with spontaneous rises in presynaptic-Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Spontaneous mito-Ca2+ loading lowers cellular NAD+/NADH redox.
source: Spontaneous mito-Ca2+ loading lowers cellular NAD+/NADH redox and downregulates ribbon size.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Spontaneous mito-Ca2+ loading downregulates ribbon size.
source: Spontaneous mito-Ca2+ loading lowers cellular NAD+/NADH redox and downregulates ribbon size.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Direct application of NAD+ increases ribbon size.
source: Direct application of NAD+ or NADH increases or decreases ribbon size respectively, possibly acting through the NAD(H)-binding domain on Ribeye.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Direct application of NADH decreases ribbon size.
source: Direct application of NAD+ or NADH increases or decreases ribbon size respectively, possibly acting through the NAD(H)-binding domain on Ribeye.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: NAD+ and NADH possibly act through the NAD(H)-binding domain on Ribeye to regulate ribbon size.
source: Direct application of NAD+ or NADH increases or decreases ribbon size respectively, possibly acting through the NAD(H)-binding domain on Ribeye.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in synaptopathies that impact neurodevelopment, learning and memory, and can contribute to neurodegeneration.
source: In neurons, mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in synaptopathies that impact neurodevelopment, learning and memory, and can contribute to neurodegeneration (Flippo and Strack, 2017; Lepeta et al., 2016; Todorova and Blokland, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hair-cell sensory neurotransmission relies on specialized ribbon synapses to facilitate rapid and sustained vesicle release that is particularly energy demanding.
source: In hair cells, sensory neurotransmission relies on specialized ribbon synapses to facilitate rapid and sustained vesicle release that is particularly energy demanding (reviewed in: Johnson et al., 2019; Lagnado and Schmitz, 2015; Matthews and Fuchs, 2010; Safieddine et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in hearing loss.
source: Although mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in hearing loss (Böttger and Schacht, 2013; Fischel-Ghodsian et al., 2004; Kokotas et al., 2007), the precise role mitochondria play at hair-cell synapses remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The precise role mitochondria play at hair-cell synapses remains unclear.
source: Although mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in hearing loss (Böttger and Schacht, 2013; Fischel-Ghodsian et al., 2004; Kokotas et al., 2007), the precise role mitochondria play at hair-cell synapses remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ribbons tether and stabilize synaptic vesicles at the active zone.
source: Ribbon synapses are characterized by a unique presynaptic structure called a 'ribbon' that tethers and stabilizes synaptic vesicles at the active zone (reviewed in: Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Neurotransmission at ribbon synapses in hair cells requires the presynaptic-Ca2+ channel CaV1.3.
source: In hair cells, neurotransmission at ribbon synapses requires the presynaptic-Ca2+ channel CaV1.3 (Brandt et al., 2003; Kollmar et al., 1997; Sidi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hair-cell depolarization opens CaV1.3 channels, resulting in a spatially restricted increase of Ca2+ at presynaptic ribbons that triggers vesicle fusion.
source: Hair-cell depolarization opens CaV1.3 channels, resulting in a spatially restricted increase of Ca2+ at presynaptic ribbons that triggers vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair cell synapse function.

claim: Tight spatial regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ is important for ribbon-synapse function.
source: Tight spatial regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ is important for ribbon-synapse function and requires efficient Ca2+ clearance through a combination of Ca2+ pumps, Ca2+ buffers and intracellular Ca2+ stores (Carafoli, 2011; Mulkey and Malenka, 1992; Tucker and Fettiplace, 1995; Yamoah et al., 1998; Zenisek and Matthews, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tight spatial regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ requires efficient Ca2+ clearance through a combination of Ca2+ pumps, Ca2+ buffers and intracellular Ca2+ stores.
source: Tight spatial regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ is important for ribbon-synapse function and requires efficient Ca2+ clearance through a combination of Ca2+ pumps, Ca2+ buffers and intracellular Ca2+ stores (Carafoli, 2011; Mulkey and Malenka, 1992; Tucker and Fettiplace, 1995; Yamoah et al., 1998; Zenisek and Matthews, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ER-Ca2+ stores have been implicated in hair-cell neurotransmission.
source: While ER-Ca2+ stores have been implicated in hair-cell neurotransmission, whether mitochondrial-Ca2+ (mito-Ca2+) stores play a role in this process remains unclear (Castellano-Muñoz and Ricci, 2014; Kennedy, 2002; Lioudyno et al., 2004; Tucker and Fettiplace, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Whether mitochondrial-Ca2+ stores play a role in hair-cell neurotransmission remains unclear.
source: While ER-Ca2+ stores have been implicated in hair-cell neurotransmission, whether mitochondrial-Ca2+ (mito-Ca2+) stores play a role in this process remains unclear (Castellano-Muñoz and Ricci, 2014; Kennedy, 2002; Lioudyno et al., 2004; Tucker and Fettiplace, 1995).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Prior to hearing onset, mammalian auditory hair cells fire spontaneous Ca2+ action potentials.
source: In mammals, prior to hearing onset, auditory hair cells fire spontaneous Ca2+ action potentials (Eckrich et al., 2018; Marcotti et al., 2003; Tritsch et al., 2007; Tritsch et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In mammalian hair cells, spontaneous Ca2+ action potentials are CaV1.3-dependent.
source: In mammalian hair cells, these Ca2+ action potentials are CaV1.3-dependent and are thought to be important for synapse and circuit formation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous Ca2+ action potentials in mammalian hair cells are thought to be important for synapse and circuit formation.
source: In mammalian hair cells, these Ca2+ action potentials are CaV1.3-dependent and are thought to be important for synapse and circuit formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on previous work.

claim: In vivo work in zebrafish hair cells found that increasing voltage-gated Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels during development led to the formation of smaller ribbons.
source: In support of this idea, in vivo work in zebrafish hair cells found that increasing or decreasing voltage-gated Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels during development led to the formation of smaller or larger ribbons respectively (Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In vivo work in zebrafish hair cells found that decreasing voltage-gated Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels during development led to the formation of larger ribbons.
source: In support of this idea, in vivo work in zebrafish hair cells found that increasing or decreasing voltage-gated Ca2+ influx through CaV1.3 channels during development led to the formation of smaller or larger ribbons respectively (Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse knockouts of CaV1.3, auditory outer hair cells have reduced afferent innervation.
source: Furthermore, in mouse knockouts of CaV1.3, auditory outer hair cells have reduced afferent innervation and synapse number (Ceriani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mouse knockouts of CaV1.3, auditory outer hair cells have reduced synapse number.
source: Furthermore, in mouse knockouts of CaV1.3, auditory outer hair cells have reduced afferent innervation and synapse number (Ceriani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: How CaV1.3-channel activity regulates ribbon size and innervation is not known.
source: Mechanistically, how CaV1.3-channel activity regulates ribbon size and innervation, and whether hair-cell Ca2+ stores play a role in this process is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Whether hair-cell Ca2+ stores play a role in regulating ribbon size and innervation is not known.
source: Mechanistically, how CaV1.3-channel activity regulates ribbon size and innervation, and whether hair-cell Ca2+ stores play a role in this process is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ribbon size varies between species and sensory epithelia.
source: Cumulative work has shown that ribbon size varies between species and sensory epithelia (reviewed in Moser et al., 2006); these variations are thought to reflect important encoding requirements of a given sensory cell (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Variations in ribbon size are thought to reflect important encoding requirements of a given sensory cell.
source: Cumulative work has shown that ribbon size varies between species and sensory epithelia (reviewed in Moser et al., 2006); these variations are thought to reflect important encoding requirements of a given sensory cell (Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In auditory hair cells, excitotoxic noise damage can alter ribbon size.
source: In auditory hair cells, excitotoxic noise damage can also alter ribbon size and lead to hearing deficits (Jensen et al., 2015; Liberman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In auditory hair cells, excitotoxic noise damage can lead to hearing deficits.
source: In auditory hair cells, excitotoxic noise damage can also alter ribbon size and lead to hearing deficits (Jensen et al., 2015; Liberman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Excitotoxic damage is thought to be initiated by mito-Ca2+ overload and subsequent ROS production.
source: Excitotoxic damage is thought to be initiated by mito-Ca2+ overload and subsequent ROS production (Böttger and Schacht, 2013; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: How ribbon size is established during development or altered under pathological conditions is not fully understood.
source: Mechanistically, precisely how ribbon size is established during development or altered under pathological conditions is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Overexpression of Ribeye in hair cells can increase ribbon size.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, previous work has shown that overexpression or depletion of Ribeye in hair cells can increase or decrease ribbon size respectively (Becker et al., 2018; Jean et al., 2018; Lv et al., 2016; Sheets, 2017; Sheets et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Depletion of Ribeye in hair cells can decrease ribbon size.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, previous work has shown that overexpression or depletion of Ribeye in hair cells can increase or decrease ribbon size respectively (Becker et al., 2018; Jean et al., 2018; Lv et al., 2016; Sheets, 2017; Sheets et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ribeye is a splice variant of the transcriptional co-repressor Carboxyl-terminal binding protein 2 (CtBP2).
source: Ribeye is a splice variant of the transcriptional co-repressor Carboxyl-terminal binding protein 2 (CtBP2) – a splice variant that is unique to vertebrate evolution (Schmitz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ribeye is a splice variant that is unique to vertebrate evolution.
source: Ribeye is a splice variant of the transcriptional co-repressor Carboxyl-terminal binding protein 2 (CtBP2) – a splice variant that is unique to vertebrate evolution (Schmitz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ribeye contains a unique A-domain and a B-domain that is nearly identical to full-length CtBP2.
source: Ribeye contains a unique A-domain and a B-domain that is nearly identical to full-length CtBP2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ribeye structure.

claim: The B-domain of Ribeye contains a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+, NADH or NAD(H)) binding site.
source: The B-domain contains a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+, NADH or NAD(H)) binding site (Magupalli et al., 2008; Schmitz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NAD(H) redox is linked to mitochondrial metabolism.
source: NAD(H) redox is linked to mitochondrial metabolism (Srivastava, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CtBPs are able to bind and detect NAD+ and NADH levels.
source: Because CtBPs are able to bind and detect NAD+ and NADH levels, they are thought to function as metabolic biosensors (Stankiewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CtBPs are thought to function as metabolic biosensors.
source: Because CtBPs are able to bind and detect NAD+ and NADH levels, they are thought to function as metabolic biosensors (Stankiewicz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Changes in NAD(H) redox can impact CtBP oligomerization.
source: For example, previous work has demonstrated that changes in NAD(H) redox can impact CtBP oligomerization and its transcriptional activity (Fjeld et al., 2003; Thio et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Changes in NAD(H) redox can impact CtBP transcriptional activity.
source: For example, previous work has demonstrated that changes in NAD(H) redox can impact CtBP oligomerization and its transcriptional activity (Fjeld et al., 2003; Thio et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In vitro work has shown that both NAD+ and NADH can promote interactions between Ribeye domains.
source: Interestingly, in vitro work has shown that both NAD+ and NADH can also promote interactions between Ribeye domains (Magupalli et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Whether NAD+ or NADH can impact Ribeye interactions and ribbon formation or stability has not been confirmed in vivo.
source: Whether NAD+ or NADH can impact Ribeye interactions and ribbon formation or stability has not been confirmed in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: During presynaptic activity, mitochondria clear and store Ca2+ at the presynapse in neurons.
source: In neurons, it is well established that during presynaptic activity, mitochondria clear and store Ca2+ at the presynapse (Devine and Kittler, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Presynaptic activity and mito-Ca2+ can couple together to influence cellular bioenergetics, including NAD(H) redox homeostasis.
source: Additionally, presynaptic activity and mito-Ca2+ can couple together to influence cellular bioenergetics, including NAD(H) redox homeostasis (reviewed in: Kann and Kovács, 2007; Llorente-Folch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Near the majority of ribbons (81%) a mitochondrion was observed in close proximity (<1 µm).
source: Near the majority of ribbons (81%) we observed a mitochondrion in close proximity (<1 µm) (Figure 1D, median ribbon-to-mitochondria distance = 174 nm, n = 17 out of 21 ribbons).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The median ribbon-to-mitochondria distance is 174 nm.
source: Near the majority of ribbons (81%) we observed a mitochondrion in close proximity (<1 µm) (Figure 1D, median ribbon-to-mitochondria distance = 174 nm, n = 17 out of 21 ribbons).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: In lateral-line hair cells, mitochondria are present near ribbons.
source: Overall our TEM and Airyscan imaging suggests that in lateral-line hair cells, mitochondria are present near ribbons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on TEM and Airyscan imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals were blocked in a dose-dependent manner after a 30 min treatment with Ru360.
source: We found that stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals were blocked in a dose-dependent manner after a 30 min treatment with Ru360 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; IC50 = 1.37 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The IC50 of Ru360 for blocking stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals is 1.37 µM.
source: We found that stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals were blocked in a dose-dependent manner after a 30 min treatment with Ru360 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; IC50 = 1.37 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A 30 min treatment with the VDAC antagonist TRO 19622 impaired stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals.
source: We observed that similar to the MCU antagonist Ru360, a 30 min treatment with the VDAC antagonist TRO 19622 also impaired stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals (10 µM TRO 19622, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Blocking CaV1.3 channels eliminated all stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals at the base of the cell.
source: Similar to blocking the MCU and VDAC, blocking CaV1.3 channels eliminated all stimulus-evoked MitoGCaMP3 signals at the base of the cell (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Isradipine specifically blocks CaV1.3 channels without impairing mechanotransduction in zebrafish hair cells.
source: Previous work in zebrafish-hair cells demonstrated that isradipine specifically blocks CaV1.3 channels without impairing mechanotransduction (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neither Ru360 nor TRO 19622 blocked mechanotransduction.
source: We measured apical, mechanically evoked Ca2+ signals in hair bundles before and after a 30 min treatment with 10 µM Ru360 or TRO 19622. Neither compound blocked mechanotransduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B'.

claim: Mito-Ca2+ uptake was only present in ~40% of cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that mito-Ca2+ uptake was only present in ~40% of cells (Examples, Figure 2A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; n = 10 neuromasts, 146 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only ~30% of hair cells within each neuromast cluster have presynaptic-Ca2+ signals and are synaptically active.
source: This observation is consistent with previous work demonstrating that only ~30% of hair cells within each neuromast cluster have presynaptic-Ca2+ signals and are synaptically active (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Two-color imaging revealed a strong correlation between the magnitude of evoked GCaMP6sCAAX and MitoRGECO1 signals.
source: Our two-color imaging approach revealed a strong correlation between the magnitude of evoked GCaMP6sCAAX and MitoRGECO1 signals (Figure 2B, R2 = 0.77, p<0.0001; n = 136 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The median MitoRGECO1 signals were 100% larger in presynaptically active hair cells compared to presynaptically silent hair cells.
source: We found that the median MitoRGECO1 signals were 100% larger in presynaptically active hair cells compared to presynaptically silent hair cells (Figure 2B').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B'.

claim: Mito-Ca2+ uptake occurs specifically in hair cells with evoked presynaptic-Ca2+ influx.
source: Together these results suggest that mito-Ca2+ uptake occurs specifically in hair cells with evoked presynaptic-Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-color imaging data.

claim: GCaMP6sCAAX signals at ribbons were reduced after complete MCU block (10 µM Ru360) during short, 200 ms stimuli.
source: We found that during short, 200 ms stimuli, GCaMP6sCAAX signals at ribbons were reduced after complete MCU block (10 µM Ru360, Figure 2C–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C–C'.

claim: Reduction of GCaMP6sCAAX signals were further exacerbated during sustained 10 s stimuli, even when the MCU was only partially blocked (2 µM Ru360).
source: Reduction of GCaMP6sCAAX signals were further exacerbated during sustained 10 s stimuli, even when the MCU was only partially blocked (2 µM Ru360, Figure 2D–D').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D–D'.

claim: A similar reduction in GCaMP6sCAAX signals were observed after a 30 min application of the VDAC inhibitor TRO 19622.
source: A similar reduction in GCaMP6sCAAX signals were observed after a 30 min application of the VDAC inhibitor TRO 19622 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E', 10 µM TRO 19622).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E'.

claim: In mature hair cells, evoked mito-Ca2+ uptake is critical for presynaptic-Ca2+ influx, especially during sustained stimulation.
source: These results suggest that in mature hair cells, evoked mito-Ca2+ uptake is critical for presynaptic-Ca2+ influx, especially during sustained stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced presynaptic-Ca2+ influx after MCU block.

claim: After a 1 hr 2 µM Ru360 treatment, Ru360 had no impact on hair cell or synapse number.
source: At this dose, Ru360 had no impact on hair cell or synapse number (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: After a 1 hr 2 µM Ru360 treatment, no morphological change in ribbon or postsynapse size was observed.
source: We also observed no morphological change in ribbon or postsynapse size (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: After the 1 hr 2 µM Ru360 treatment, CaV1.3 clusters were still present at synapses, but the channels were at a significantly higher density compared to controls.
source: After the 1 hr 2 µM Ru360 treatment, CaV1.3 clusters were still present at synapses, but the channels were at a significantly higher density compared to controls (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E–H.

claim: In mature hair cells, partial MCU block may impair presynaptic function by altering CaV1.3 channel density.
source: These findings indicate that in mature hair cells, partial MCU block may impair presynaptic function by altering CaV1.3 channel density.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing altered CaV1.3 channel density after partial MCU block.

claim: After a 30 min treatment with 10 µM Ru360, ribbons were significantly larger.
source: But after the 30 min treatment, ribbons were significantly larger (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: After a 1 hr, 10 µM Ru360 treatment, there were both fewer hair cells per neuromast and fewer synapses per hair cell.
source: After 1 hr, there were both fewer hair cells per neuromast (Hair cells per neuromast, control: 18.1, 1 hr 10 µM Ru360: 12.0; p>0.0001) and fewer synapses per hair cell (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: After 1 hr 10 µM Ru360 treatment, ribbons were significantly larger.
source: Similar to 30 min treatments with Ru360, after 1 hr, ribbons were also significantly larger (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Neither 30 min nor 1 hr 10 µM Ru360 treatment altered postsynapse size.
source: Neither 30 min nor 1 hr 10 µM Ru360 treatment altered postsynapse size (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In mature hair cells, partial block of mito-Ca2+ uptake may impair presynaptic function by altering CaV1.3 channel clustering, without seemingly altering other gross pre- or post-synaptic morphology.
source: Overall, our results indicate that in mature hair cells, partial block of mito-Ca2+ uptake may impair presynaptic function by altering CaV1.3 channel clustering, without seemingly altering other gross pre- or post-synaptic morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing altered CaV1.3 channel clustering without other morphological changes after partial MCU block.

claim: Complete block of mito-Ca2+ uptake is pathological; it impairs presynaptic function, alters presynaptic morphology, and results in a loss of synapses and hair-cells.
source: Complete block of mito-Ca2+ uptake is pathological; it impairs presynaptic function, alters presynaptic morphology, and results in a loss of synapses and hair-cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing pathological effects after complete MCU block.

claim: Mammalian hair cells have spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ influx during development.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated that mammalian hair cells have spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ influx during development (Eckrich et al., 2018; Holman et al., 2019; Marcotti et al., 2003; Tritsch et al., 2007; Tritsch et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In developing hair cells, spontaneous GCaMP6sCAAX signals occurred with larger magnitudes and at a higher frequency compared to those in mature hair cells.
source: We found that in developing hair cells, spontaneous GCaMP6sCAAX signals occurred with larger magnitudes and at a higher frequency compared to those in mature hair cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Similar to mammals, spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ activity is a feature of developing zebrafish hair cells.
source: Our spontaneous GCaMP6sCAAX imaging demonstrates that similar to mammals, spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ activity is a feature of developing zebrafish hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ activity in developing zebrafish hair cells.

claim: Spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ influx was often associated with spontaneous mito-Ca2+ uptake.
source: We found that spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ influx was often associated with spontaneous mito-Ca2+ uptake (Example, Figure 4A–A''').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A–A'''.

claim: A high correlation was observed between the rise and fall of spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ and mito-Ca2+ signals within individual cells.
source: Overall, we observed a high correlation between the rise and fall of these two signals within individual cells (Figure 4A''–A''').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A''–A'''.

claim: Both spontaneous presynaptic-Ca2+ and mito-Ca2+ signals and their correlation were abolished by application of the CaV1.3-channel antagonist isradipine.
source: Both of these signals and their correlation were abolished by application of the CaV1.3-channel antagonist isradipine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similar to evoked experiments, spontaneous presynaptic- and mito-Ca2+ signals are correlated.
source: Together these experiments indicate that, similar to our evoked experiments, spontaneous presynaptic- and mito-Ca2+ signals are correlated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing correlation between spontaneous presynaptic- and mito-Ca2+ signals.

claim: CaV1.3 channel activity plays a role in regulating ribbon size specifically during development in zebrafish.
source: Previous work in zebrafish demonstrated that CaV1.3 channel activity plays a role in regulating ribbon size specifically during development (Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A transient, 1 hr pharmacological block of CaV1.3 channels increased ribbon size.
source: This work found that a transient, 1 hr pharmacological block of CaV1.3 channels increased ribbon size, while CaV1.3 channel agonists decreased ribbon size (Figure 5E; Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 5E.

claim: CaV1.3 channel agonists decreased ribbon size.
source: This work found that a transient, 1 hr pharmacological block of CaV1.3 channels increased ribbon size, while CaV1.3 channel agonists decreased ribbon size (Figure 5E; Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 5E.

claim: After a 1 hr application of 2 μM Ru360 to block the MCU, a significant increase in ribbon size was observed in developing hair cells.
source: After a 1 hr application of 2 μM Ru360 to block the MCU, we observed a significant increase in ribbon size in developing hair cells (Figure 5A–B,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A–B,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A 1 hr 2 µM Ru360 treatment did not impact ribbon size in mature hair cells.

claim: In developing hair cells, after a 1 hr 10 µM Ru360 treatment, a significant increase in ribbon size was observed.

claim: In developing hair cells, MCU antagonist concentrations did not alter the number of hair cells or the number of synapses per hair cell.

claim: MCU block did not alter the size of the postsynapse in developing hair cells.

claim: At higher concentrations of Ru360 (10 µM), an increase in cytoplasmic, non-synaptic Ribeye aggregates was observed.

claim: CaV1.3a-deficient hair cells have both larger ribbons and cytoplasmic aggregates of Ribeye.

claim: During development, spontaneous Ca2+ entry through both CaV1.3 and MCU channels continuously regulate ribbon formation.

claim: Blocking either CaV1.3 or MCU channels increases Ribeye aggregation and ribbon size during development.
source: Our results suggest that during development, spontaneous Ca2+ entry through both CaV1.3 and MCU channels continuously regulate ribbon formation; blocking either channel increases Ribeye aggregation and ribbon size.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased ribbon size and Ribeye aggregation after blocking CaV1.3 or MCU channels.

claim: Treatment with the CaV1.3 channel antagonist isradipine decreased resting CytoRGECO1 fluorescence.
source: We observed that treatment with the CaV1.3 channel antagonist isradipine and agonist Bay K8644 decreased and increased resting CytoRGECO1 fluorescence respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with the CaV1.3 channel agonist Bay K8644 increased resting CytoRGECO1 fluorescence.
source: We observed that treatment with the CaV1.3 channel antagonist isradipine and agonist Bay K8644 decreased and increased resting CytoRGECO1 fluorescence respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: MCU function and associated mito-Ca2+ uptake does not play a critical role in buffering steady state cyto-Ca2+ levels.

claim: Blocking CaV1.3 channels with isradipine decreased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence.
source: We observed that blocking CaV1.3 channels with isradipine or the MCU with Ru360 decreased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 6E–F).

claim: Blocking the MCU with Ru360 decreased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence.
source: We observed that blocking CaV1.3 channels with isradipine or the MCU with Ru360 decreased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6E–F.

claim: CaV1.3 channel agonist Bay K8644 increased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence.
source: Conversely, CaV1.3 channel agonist Bay K8644 increased resting MitoGCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 6E).

claim: The effects of CaV1.3 channel and MCU activity converge to regulate mito-Ca2+ levels.

claim: When either CaV1.3 or MCU channels are blocked, the resting levels of mito-Ca2+ decrease.

claim: If presynaptic-Ca2+ influx and mito-Ca2+ regulate ribbon size through a similar mechanism, they may act through mito- rather than cyto-Ca2+ homeostasis.
source: Therefore, if presynaptic-Ca2+ influx and mito-Ca2+ regulate ribbon size through a similar mechanism, they may act through mito- rather than cyto-Ca2+ homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data showing that mito-Ca2+ but not cyto-Ca2+ levels are affected by both CaV1.3 and MCU activity.

claim: Ribeye protein contains a putative NAD(H) binding site.

claim: Mitochondria regulate NAD(H) redox homeostasis.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Incubation with 100 µM NAD+ increased Rex-YFP fluorescence.

claim: Incubation with 5 mM NADH decreased Rex-YFP fluorescence.

claim: 30 min treatments with either a CaV1.3 or MCU channel antagonist increased the NAD+/NADH ratio in developing hair cells.

claim: Similar 30 min treatments did not alter Rex-YFP fluorescence in mature hair cells.

claim: During development, CaV1.3 and MCU channel activities normally function to increase mito-Ca2+ and decrease the NAD+/NADH ratio.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that blocking CaV1.3 or MCU channels decreases mito-Ca2+ and increases the NAD+/NADH ratio.

claim: This work provides strong evidence that links NAD(H) redox and mito-Ca2+ with ribbon formation.
source: Overall, this work provides strong evidence that links NAD(H) redox and mito-Ca2+ with ribbon formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that mito-Ca2+ and NAD(H) redox are linked to ribbon formation.

claim: After a 1 hr treatment with 100 µM NAD+, the ribbons in developing hair cells were significantly larger compared to controls.

claim: After a 1 hr treatment with 5 mM NADH, ribbons were significantly smaller compared to controls.
source: In contrast, after a 1 hr treatment with 5 mM NADH, ribbons were significantly smaller compared to controls (Figure 7A,C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A,C,E.

claim: Neither exogenous NAD+ nor NADH were able to alter ribbon size in mature hair cells.

claim: NAD+ and NADH concentrations altered neither the number of synapses per hair cell nor postsynapse size in developing or mature hair cells.

claim: In developing hair cells, NAD+ promotes while NADH inhibits Ribeye-Ribeye interactions or Ribeye localization to the ribbon.
source: These results suggest that in developing hair cells, NAD+ promotes while NADH inhibits Ribeye-Ribeye interactions or Ribeye localization to the ribbon.

claim: During development, the levels of NAD+ and NADH can directly regulate ribbon size in vivo.
source: Overall these results support the idea that during development, the levels of NAD+ and NADH can directly regulate ribbon size in vivo.

claim: In mature hair cells, blocking presynaptic- and mito-Ca2+ activities was pathological and did not influence NAD(H) redox.

source: Similar to our results in developing hair cells, in cardiac myocytes, mito-Ca2+ drives cellular metabolism, which reduces NAD+ to NADH (Bertero and Maack, 2018).
